title: The small-business audience and AI adoption
introduction: A large business base, uneven adoption, and a continuing need for practical guidance. These figures provide context for the scenarios below; they do not forecast readership, conversions, or revenue.

cards.body: SBA’s February 2026 report counts 36,207,130 businesses with fewer than 500 employees.
cards.footnote: The 2022 total includes 29,811,495 nonemployer firms (82.3%) and 6,395,635 employer firms.

implementationNeeds.title: Explain where to start
implementationNeeds.body: 16% of surveyed nonusers cited insufficient AI knowledge.
implementationNeeds.interpretation: Editorial implication: teach one concrete task with a worked example, prerequisites, and a way to check the result. This is a topic-selection rationale, not measured demand for this website.

implementationNeeds.title: Make data choices understandable
implementationNeeds.body: 27% of surveyed nonusers worried about exposing sensitive data.
implementationNeeds.interpretation: Editorial implication: explain which information a workflow needs, offer fictional examples, and show where owners should review permissions and vendor data settings. Concern alone does not establish purchase intent.

methodology.shortNote: These sources use different populations, questions, and dates. Survey percentages are estimates, not counts of potential customers.
methodology.nonUserCountNote: There is no directly comparable nationwide count of small businesses not using AI in these sources. SBA includes businesses without employees; Census’s AI survey covers employers; the Chamber uses a different business-size definition. Multiplying an AI nonuse percentage by 36.2 million would produce an unsupported estimate.
rules: Keep the population and fieldwork date visible with every adoption percentage.
Show 34% as a calculated complement within one survey, not as a separate survey finding or count.
Do not treat the two complementary adoption cards as two independent pieces of evidence.
Do not interpret nonuse as unmet demand, readiness to buy, or an inevitable future conversion.
Keep observed statistics separate from editorial implications and the visitor’s economic scenario inputs.
Do not infer a causal effect on growth or a guaranteed educational or financial result from descriptive survey evidence.

surveyComparability.summary: The research definition is an independent business with fewer than 500 employees. The February 2026 publication combines 2022 Statistics of U.S. Businesses and Nonemployer Statistics; publication year is not the count’s reference year.
Online survey: 3,732 U.S. businesses, fewer than 250 employees; July 23–August 6, 2026. Published October 2. Readiness includes self-directed learning; the chart records 5% doing nothing.

BTOS represents nonfarm employer businesses, including firms larger than the small-business thresholds. It asks about AI use during the previous two weeks. Wording broadened from producing goods/services to any business function in late 2025; the old and revised questions should not be plotted as an unchanged measure. The October 22, 2026 release covers the period ending October 18. Its latest numeric AI estimate was not extracted, so no October adoption rate is displayed.

NFIB’s June 25, 2025 release concerns small employers from its membership survey. Fieldwork ran March 6–31, 2025: 20,000 owners invited, 521 completed. The AI item has 514 employer responses: 24% yes and 76% no. These older, differently sampled results are context, not a second estimate of the Chamber’s 2026 population.

Observed transactions for 4.6 million Chase Business Banking firms over 2019–2025. The 27.5% statistic is conditional on paying for AI during 2025 and counts distinct services paid for during that year. It is not a share of all U.S. businesses or a measure of newly attributed affiliate purchases.

The 2024 nonemployer-establishment count is newer than SBA’s combined 2022 benchmark. It describes a segment with a defined receipts threshold and is presented separately, without mixing years into a new national total.

methodology.selectionNote: Headline cards use the latest consolidated SBA FAQ located and the current Chamber original report. Census and NFIB are retained to make the population differences explicit. No all-business nonuser count is supplied.
methodology.maintenanceTrigger: Review when SBA issues a new national count or the Chamber releases a new edition. Any replacement adoption estimate must retain its own definition, reference period, and denominator.
methodology.marketShareNote: Market-share percentages are chosen scenario assumptions applied to a dated business-count benchmark. They are not survey-estimated conversion probabilities. National penetration counts unique U.S. businesses, while qualifying vendor purchases and commission payments are separate measures.
methodology.spendingComparability: The Chamber’s $250 median concerns self-reported AI spending among its 2026 paying respondents. JPMorganChase Institute’s approximately $28–$30 median concerns identifiable AI payments in its 2025 business banking data. Neither is an average across all U.S. businesses, and the measures should not be pooled.
methodology.nonemployerUpdate: Census’s September 29, 2026 release reports 31,985,874 nonemployer establishments for 2024. SBA’s consolidated 36,207,130 total remains a 2022 benchmark. The newer component is kept separate rather than combined with an older employer count.

editorialInterpretation.label: Interpretation, not a survey finding
editorialInterpretation.text: The case for this publication is helping owners understand a task, choose a suitable tool, and implement it with confidence. Adoption gaps and learning needs help shape that work. They do not establish how many owners will visit this site or buy through its links.
editorialInterpretation.modelBoundary: Use explicit market-share, traffic, purchase, commission, refund, retention and payout assumptions. A target share can be translated into required business acquisitions and traffic; national business counts are not evidence that those customers have been acquired.

marketShare.definition: Independent U.S. businesses with fewer than 500 employees, including employer and nonemployer firms. This is a broad reference population, not a verified pool of paying customers.
marketShare.countingRule: Count each acquired business once for market penetration. Several qualifying vendor purchases by that business can generate separate commissions without becoming additional businesses.
marketShare.interpretation: The opportunity includes first-time adopters and businesses adding or replacing tools. AI use does not mean a business has finished choosing software; eligibility for commission depends on each vendor’s new-customer and attribution rules.

evidence.title: Businesses already pay for several AI services
evidence.body: Among AI-paying firms in JPMorganChase Institute’s 2025 transaction data, 18.06% paid for two services and 9.44% for three or more. The sum supports exploring multiple purchases; it does not establish three purchases per business or attribution to one publisher.

evidence.title: Observed AI payments in a banking dataset
evidence.body: Approximate 2025 median in JPMorganChase Institute’s payment analysis. It covers identifiable paid AI services, excluding free use, custom development and AI embedded in other software. It is not the median software budget of every U.S. business.

evidence.title: Self-reported AI spending among paying users
evidence.body: Median reported by businesses paying for AI in the Chamber’s 2026 survey. This differs from the banking study in year, sample and measurement. The two figures are separate reference points, not a blended market average or fully commissionable spending.

evidence.title: A newer count of businesses without employees
evidence.body: Census counted these nonemployer establishments in 2024; the data were released September 29, 2026. This newer segment count is shown separately. It is not added to the older employer count to create an unsupported national total.
